newsitem.title: INDIA: India's new PM promises business as usual.
newsitem.headline: India's new PM promises business as usual.

text.p: India's new prime minister, Inder Kumar Gujral, took power on Monday after a three-week crisis promising business as usual and appointing a near carbon-copy cabinet modelled on his fallen predecessor's.
In his maiden policy speech, Gujral moved swiftly to allay concerns he might slow down economic reforms that have opened the second most populous nation to trade and investment.

The 77-year-old Marxist-turned-social democrat threw his support behind a landmark budget that revived stock markets when it was introduced in February but had been held hostage by a three-week political crisis in the Indian capital.
In a sign of his commitment to continuity, Gujral stepped up efforts to seduce the architect of the budget, departing finance minister P. Chidambaram, into his council of ministers.

Gujral, a veteran statesman and two-time foreign minister, gave every indication the government's goals had changed very little despite three weeks of turmoil which toppled the previous prime minister and brought the nation to the brink of mid-term polls.
"It is business as usual," he told several hundred business leaders only hours after he assumed office in a ceremony at the British-built Presidential Palace.

Gujral's reassurances shored up stock markets, which had had their fill of uncertainty since March 30 when Congress party president Sitaram Kesri unexpectedly revoked his support for Deve Gowda, triggering the crisis that was now on the wane.
The Bombay bourse index, confident Chidambaram's budget would make it safely through parliament, surged 2.8 percent on Monday to close at a provisional 3,799.79 points.
"In Mr Gujral, the market is quite hopeful," said Neeraj Roy, head of institutional sales at Prime Broking in Bombay.
Gujral reappointed all but five ministers from Deve Gowda's fallen government to their same posts, leaving 35 in place.

The five outsiders included four from Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress party, which on Saturday said it would not join the government because the 15-party United Front passed over its leader G.K. Moopanar in choosing a new chief.

But the alliance, keen to patch over the embarrassing split, launched a campaign to win back Moopanar and Chidambaram, who was Deve Gowda's most articulate spokesman for free-market reforms which many leftwing partners in the United Front still find hard to swallow.
Moopanar showed signs of wavering, saying it was up to his party colleagues to decide whether to join the cabinet.
Gujral kept the finance portfolio for himself -- so that he could give it back to Chidambaram if he returned to the fold.

The new prime minister was set to face a vote of confidence in parliament on Tuesday at around 5 p.m. (1230 GMT). He was assured victory because he had the support of the United Front's 178 votes in the 542-member lower house as well as Congress's 140.

Congress helped to topple Deve Gowda, and while Gujral has established a coordination committee aimed at improving communication between the United Front and Congress, his alliance is still beholden to its uneasy ally.
Gujral's rivals predicted a rocky road for the head of the centre-left coalition, which came close to rupturing during three days of frantic lobbying by ambitious aspirants.
"The prime minister is likely to have a trying time to keep heterogenous elements together," K.L. Sharma, a spokesman for the rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party, said.
"I gave the last government one year in office," BJP president L.K. Advani said. "And I don't give them any more."

In a clear sign of his desire to allay industry's worries, the goateed, bespectacled prime minister who made his political start when India was still a socialist economy said he would press ahead with economic reforms.
"India can look forward to the continuation of reform and programmes, and its deepening and widening," he told the Confederation of Indian Industry.

The new prime minister, who kept the foreign ministry portfolio for himself, promised to continue his policy of building better relations with India's neighbours including old foe Pakistan. India's neighbours were pleased.

Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina called Gujral a "genuine friend". Pakistani newspapers were fulsome in praise. Sri Lanka called him an old friend. President Chandrika Kumaratunga said "there could be no more fitting choice to lead India in this, its 50th anniversary year of independence".
